title: 3-Read Friday #11: Pre-Questions, Testing Motivation, and If-Then Statements
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #11 curates three posts on the science of studying and how knowledge is structured for learning. Andrew Watson reports on a new Soderstrom and Bjork study showing that "prequestions" -- asking students about material before it is taught -- boost learning of both directly and indirectly related content, provided the technique is used sparingly and does not activate a prior misconception. Matthew Evans unpacks the motivational theory behind testing, arguing that low-stakes quizzing works not just to check knowledge but to build students' volition to study through experienced success, correct attribution of effort, and mastery goals. Ollie Lovell proposes reframing classroom knowledge as nested "if-then" statements, so that students understand not just what they are doing but why and when to apply it. Barton frames all three as reminders that assessment and retrieval are levers for motivation and understanding, not simply measurement tools.
points: Prequestions work best when used rarely, at the start of a unit on the most important concepts, and only where they will not activate a false sense of already knowing the answer.
Testing motivates productive study not merely by measuring knowledge but by building students' expectancy of success, correct attribution of success to effort, and a sense of mastery.
Framing taught content as "if-then" statements -- if you want outcome Y, then you can take action X -- gives students an explicit answer to why and when, not just what, they are learning.
Barton's throughline: assessment devices such as prequestions, low-stakes quizzes, and retrieval questions are motivational and structural tools for learning, not just checks for understanding.
quotes: Pre-testing is one of those ideas that appears to be supported by research, but I just cannot seem to make it work in the maths classroom.
Andrew provides a really good summary of the paper, as well as some super practical implications and caveats for classroom practice.
Whilst the students were reluctant at first, once they realised that regular quizzing was helping them remember things better, their enthusiasm and enjoyment of the quiz grew and grew.
Anyway, Matthew’s blog, more than anything else I have ever read, gets to the bottom of how to tap into the potential for quizzes to be motivational.
Ollie suggests that we think of how we frame concepts we teach students as if-then statements.
Being explicit with these if-then statements is useful for our planning, but also for helping students recognise the purpose of what they are learning.
